teaser.text: Associated British Foods (ABF) is a group of food, ingredients, sugar, agriculture and clothing businesses, with Primark as its largest single business. It earns money from shoppers and companies, then spends that money on products, crops, factories, stores, staff and delivery.

stock.meta_description: ABF stock forecast: weighted scenarios point to a near-term loss before recovery, driven by Primark, Sugar and the separation.
stock.opening: ABF’s weighted price is 1779.64 GBp in October 2027, a 5% total-return loss with dividends. It hinges on Primark converting expansion into cash.
stock.closing: The full memo also answers what ABF’s business, rivals, management and risks mean for the shares.

paragraphs.text: The forecast points to a small near-term loss followed by recovery. The weighted price is 1779.64 GBp in October 2027, a 5% total-return loss with dividends. It reaches 1978.11 GBp in October 2028, an 8% gain, and 2248.39 GBp in October 2029, a 25% gain.

The 2029 range is unusually wide for a mature retailer and food group. The bear case gives 1275.43 GBp, while the bull case gives 3887.59 GBp. Today’s price is 1942.50 GBp. The forecast assigns 30% to bear, 55% to base and 15% to bull, because the evidence supports recovery but also shows material Sugar and Primark risks.

blocks.heading: What has to go right or wrong for ABF?

paragraphs.text: The forecast assigns 30% probability to the bear case, 55% to the base case and 15% to the bull case. The bear case combines weak Primark stores with heavy Sugar losses. The base case assumes gradual earnings recovery and valuation expansion only as execution becomes clearer. The bull case requires stronger store demand and faster Sugar recovery.

blocks.heading: How much cash does ABF really make?

paragraphs.text: For 2025, cash from operations was **£2,231m**, but working capital tied up **£95m**. Capital spending and lease payments then reduced the amount available, leaving free cash flow of **£638m**. ABF’s own measure was **£648m**, because its definition makes different adjustments.

blocks.heading: What does an investor pay for ABF today?

paragraphs.text: A price-to-earnings ratio, or P/E, says how much investors pay for each pound of annual profit. The trailing multiple uses the latest year’s earnings; the forward multiple uses expected earnings over the next year. A lower forward multiple therefore means analysts expect profit to rise. Imagine buying a shop for £100 when it earned £7 last year: that is about fourteen times earnings. If it is expected to earn £8 next year, the price has not changed but the multiple falls to about twelve and a half times. The forecast can be wrong because sugar profits move with prices, crops and energy costs.

blocks.heading: How much does ABF pay in dividends?

paragraphs.text: Dividends remain cautious because cash demands compete with shareholder returns. Base DPS stays at £0.63 through the first two periods. It reaches £0.65 in the third. The bear case cuts DPS to £0.50 and then £0.40, while the bull case rises to £0.65, £0.70 and £0.75. The base follows the 63.0p ordinary dividend and the maintained 20.7p interim. The bear case reflects 2025 dividends of £656m against free cash flow of £638m.

blocks.heading: Does ABF's dividend have cash cover?

paragraphs.text: For 2025, cash from operations was **£2,231m**, but working capital tied up **£95m**. Capital spending and lease payments then reduced the amount available, leaving free cash flow of **£638m**. ABF’s own measure was **£648m**, because its definition makes different adjustments.

Shareholder payments have sometimes exceeded the cash generated in the same year. Free cash flow is the surplus after running the business and funding necessary investment; dividends and buybacks are separate choices to return money to shareholders. ABF completed a £500 million buyback programme in August 2025 and announced another £250 million programme for the following financial year.

blocks.heading: What is ABF's dividend yield against its share price?

paragraphs.text: The hurdle can be made concrete. If an investor wanted a 10% total return in a year, kept the P/E unchanged and received the current 3.2% dividend yield, earnings would need to grow by roughly 6.8%. A changed dividend, a lower multiple or a disappointing forecast would alter that requirement.

The 2029 range is unusually wide for a mature retailer and food group. The bear case gives 1275.43 GBp, while the bull case gives 3887.59 GBp. Today’s price is 1942.50 GBp. earnings.opening: ABF's next results are expected on November 3, 2026. Watch whether Primark's new stores offset weaker like-for-like sales while its margin holds.
earnings.closing: The full ABF memo also covers its business, rivals, management and risks.

blocks.heading: What has ABF guided for the year?

paragraphs.text: Management expects Primark sales growth of 2% in 2026 despite like-for-like sales down 2.6%, with new stores contributing 5% to growth. For 2027, it targets a 4% contribution from new space and an adjusted operating margin around 10%. Sugar guidance allows for a 2027 adjusted operating loss of £70 million to £170 million.

blocks.heading: Did ABF meet its past performance test?

paragraphs.text: The longer-term Restricted Share Plan, or RSP, works over roughly three years. Its “underpin” is a minimum test: even if the award is not tied to one simple formula, the committee can reduce it if overall performance does not justify the shares. For the first cycle, covering 2022–25, the committee said the underpin was met. It cited average return on capital of 16.11% and earnings-per-share growth of 33% over the three-year period.

blocks.heading: What should ABF watch in the next results?

paragraphs.text: The first checkpoint is the 2026 annual-results announcement scheduled for 3 November 2026. It should show where Sugar’s loss landed within its guidance, whether group adjusted earnings per share came in ahead as expected, and whether Primark’s new stores compensated for weaker like-for-like sales while its margin held.

The larger test is Sugar in 2027. European prices, gas, the UK beet crop, African production, weather and currencies will determine whether the loss is nearer the mild or severe end of management’s range. At the same time, ABF must control separation costs and show that Primark and Food can stand alone as the planned December 2027 demerger approaches.
